title: Empirically Grounded Agent-Based Models of Innovation Diffusion: A Critical Review
publisher: arXiv (cs.SI), Zhang & Vorobeychik, Vanderbilt University; v4 25 May 2017

key_points.claim: Traditional aggregate models (Bass) assume homogeneous, fully connected populations; ABM adds agent heterogeneity and network-mediated interaction.
key_points.evidence_quote: The ABM paradigm offers two advantages for the study of innovation diffusion: first, it facilitates the modeling of agent heterogeneity, and second, it enables fine-grained modeling of interactions mediated by social networks.

key_points.claim: Classic ABMs were conceptual and simple ('toy models'). Policy use is pushing a shift to empirically grounded models, where data initialize, parameterize or validate the simulation.
key_points.evidence_quote: In these studies, empirical data are used to initialize simulation, parameterize agent-based models, or to evaluate model validity.

key_points.claim: Taxonomy of agent decision/adoption models: six methodological categories.
key_points.evidence_quote: mathematical optimization based models, economic models, cognitive agent models, heuristic models, statistics-based models and social influence models

key_points.claim: Calibration is split into micro-calibration (individual data, e.g. surveys for cognitive models like Theory of Planned Behavior) and macro-calibration (fitting aggregate diffusion trajectories, common for heuristic and economic models).
key_points.evidence_quote: we call the first kind of calibration "micro-calibration", as it uses individual data during calibration, whereas the second type "macro-calibration", as it uses aggregate-level data.

key_points.claim: Issue I: macro-calibration risks over-fitting because ABMs are non-linear and aggregate data are limited. Remedies: parameter zones, multiple indicators, pattern-oriented modeling.
key_points.evidence_quote: many parameter variations can give rise to similar aggregate dynamics.

key_points.claim: Issue II: validation on independent data is often informal, incomplete or missing. Few reviewed papers follow formal validation approaches.
key_points.evidence_quote: validation is often informal, incomplete, and even missing.

key_points.claim: Issue III: few studies validate at both micro and macro level. The authors argue that accurate aggregate predictions need accurate individual behavior, and they recommend cross-validation.
key_points.evidence_quote: robust predictions at the aggregate level can only emerge when individual behavior is accurately modeled as well

key_points.claim: Issue IV: few studies test forecasting on independent future data. The authors propose 'forward validation' with a temporal split of the data.
key_points.evidence_quote: calibration is performed on data prior to a split date, and forward validation is done on data after the split date

key_points.claim: Recommended maximum likelihood estimation, borrowed from information-diffusion modeling, as a principled way to calibrate probabilistic agent adoption models on individual-level data.
key_points.evidence_quote: we recommend constructing probabilistic adoption models for agents, and estimating parameters of these models by maximizing a global likelihood function

key_points.claim: Most standard-practice pitfalls (Richiardi et al. protocol) are largely addressed in the reviewed work: theory, model description, sensitivity analysis, formal representations (UML/ODD) and public code.
key_points.evidence_quote: nearly all of the reviewed papers present theoretical background, related work, sufficient description of model structure, sensitivity analysis of parameter variability, a formal representation

key_points.claim: Summary of validation frameworks: Carley's four levels (grounding, calibration, verification, harmonizing) and Rand & Rust's four validation steps (micro-face, macro-face, empirical input, empirical output).
key_points.evidence_quote: Carley (1996) suggests four levels of validation: grounding, calibration, verification, and harmonizing.

reliability_notes: Full text was read (a 41-page PDF, decoded from base64). This is a peer-style critical review by credible authors, but it is about innovation diffusion, a narrow slice of artificial societies. Its methodology (calibration and validation) generalizes to social ABMs. I read the intro, discussion and conclusions in detail, and did not read the per-category application sections in detail.
